title: If You Don't Know Me by Now

meta.title: Who originally recorded "If You Don't Know Me by Now"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Simply Red. Harold Melvin & the Blue Notes cut it first, in 1972 on Philadelphia International, written by Kenny Gamble and Leon Huff.
meta.ogTitle: Who originally recorded 'If You Don't Know Me by Now'?
meta.ogDescription: Simply Red's 1989 hit is a cover. Harold Melvin & the Blue Notes released it in 1972 — a No. 1 R&B single sung by Teddy Pendergrass.

answer.label: Not a Simply Red original — a 1972 Harold Melvin & the Blue Notes single
answer.originalArtistDates: Philadelphia vocal group, formed mid-1950s; hits era led by Teddy Pendergrass (1950-2010)
answer.sourceLine: A great many listeners first met this song through Simply Red and file it as theirs. It was already a hit long before: Harold Melvin & the Blue Notes released it as a Philadelphia International single on 11 September 1972 ↗, with Teddy Pendergrass on lead. It was written and produced by Kenny Gamble and Leon Huff, who had first intended it for Labelle — a group that never recorded it. Far from obscure, the original went to No. 1 on the US R&B chart and No. 3 on the Hot 100.

original.heading: Who recorded it first
original.label: Philadelphia International Records
original.released: Issued as a single on Philadelphia International Records on 11 September 1972, backed with “Let Me Into Your World”, and carried on the album I Miss You (US, August 1972, catalogue KZ 31648). Recorded at Sigma Sound in Philadelphia.
original.charted: A major hit on release: No. 1 on the US R&B chart and No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100. This was the group’s breakthrough single.
original.cover: Simply Red’s version, produced by Stewart Levine, was released on 27 March 1989 on WEA and Elektra from the album A New Flame. It reached No. 1 in the US, Australia and New Zealand and No. 2 in the UK, and the song won Best R&B Song at the 1990 Grammy ceremony — an award to writers Gamble and Huff.

trail: The single’s release date, label, B-side, Sigma Sound recording location and chart peaks are all set out on the song’s Wikipedia entry ↗, which also records that the song was written for Labelle and never recorded by them.
The 1972 US pressing of I Miss You on Philadelphia International, catalogue KZ 31648, is catalogued at MusicBrainz ↗ with the song at track four and “Let Me Into Your World” at track six.
That the 1990 Grammy for Best R&B Song went to Gamble and Huff — not to the performers — is confirmed in the award’s winners list ↗, which states the award goes to the songwriter.

authors.name: Harold Melvin & the Blue Notes
authors.heading: Harold Melvin & the Blue Notes
authors.metaLine: Philadelphia soul group; Harold Melvin 1929-1997, lead vocal by Teddy Pendergrass 1950-2010
authors.bio: The Blue Notes had been working Philadelphia since the mid-1950s, founded by Harold Melvin, long before anything stuck. What changed everything was Teddy Pendergrass, who joined in 1970 as a drummer in the backing band and was promoted to lead singer the same year. “If You Don’t Know Me by Now” was the group’s first hit and the record that made Pendergrass a star — No. 1 R&B, No. 3 pop, cut at Sigma Sound with Gamble and Huff producing.

authors.name: Simply Red
authors.heading: Simply Red
authors.metaLine: British band formed in Manchester, 1985; fronted by Mick Hucknall
authors.bio: Simply Red formed in Manchester in 1985 and put their reading of the song on A New Flame, released as a single on 27 March 1989 through WEA and Elektra and produced by Stewart Levine. It became the band’s second US No. 1 and one of the biggest international singles of that year. It is a genuinely lovely vocal performance, and the band never claimed to have written it — the only error is chronological, and it belongs to the audience rather than to Mick Hucknall.

authors.name: Kenny Gamble and Leon Huff
authors.heading: Kenny Gamble and Leon Huff
authors.metaLine: Kenny Gamble b. 11 August 1943; Leon Huff b. 8 April 1942; founders of Philadelphia International Records
authors.bio: Gamble and Huff wrote and produced the song, and founded Philadelphia International Records in 1971 as a deliberate rival to Motown. They were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in March 2008 as the first recipients of the Ahmet Ertegun Award for non-performers. The Simply Red version won them a Grammy for Best R&B Song at the 1990 ceremony — a songwriter’s award, which is why the trophy went to the two men who had written the song in the first place.

misattribution.heading: Right song, wrong origin
misattribution.intro: The song is regularly filed as a Simply Red original. It was a hit record before that band existed.

items.who: Simply Red wrote and originated it
items.why: Their version was released on 27 March 1989 on WEA and Elektra, from the album A New Flame. It is a cover, and a hugely successful one — No. 1 in the US, Australia and New Zealand.
Released as a Philadelphia International single on 11 September 1972, recorded at Sigma Sound with Teddy Pendergrass on lead vocal. It reached No. 1 R&B and No. 3 on the Hot 100.
They wrote and produced it, and their names are on both records. The song was first intended for Labelle, who never recorded it.

misattribution.truthLine: Simply Red made it famous a second time. Harold Melvin & the Blue Notes made it famous first.

context.heading: Why the cover eclipsed the original
lead: The interesting thing here is that the original was not a flop waiting to be rescued. It was a No. 1 R&B record and a top-three pop hit, the song that broke Harold Melvin & the Blue Notes nationally and announced Teddy Pendergrass. Nothing about it needed finding.

What happened instead is a generational handover. Simply Red’s A New Flame arrived in 1989 into a radio format — and a music-video economy — that recycled its catalogue constantly, and a whole cohort met the song there first. Add a songwriting Grammy attached to the 1989 record and the newer version acquires the aura of the definitive one. The credit line on the sleeve always said Gamble and Huff; most people simply never read it.
detailsBody: Gamble and Huff write the song, intending it for Labelle. Labelle never record it.
The song goes instead to Harold Melvin & the Blue Notes, with Teddy Pendergrass on lead vocal, recorded at Sigma Sound in Philadelphia.
11 September 1972 — released as a Philadelphia International single, backed with “Let Me Into Your World”, and carried on the album I Miss You.
The single reaches No. 1 on the US R&B chart and No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100.
Patti LaBelle — for whose group the song was originally written — performs a live version on her 1985 album Patti.
27 March 1989 — Simply Red release their version, from A New Flame, on WEA and Elektra; it reaches No. 1 in the US, Australia and New Zealand and No. 2 in the UK.
At the 1990 Grammy ceremony the song wins Best R&B Song. The award goes to the songwriters, Gamble and Huff.
Later readings include Seal on Soul (2008) and Martina McBride on Everlasting (2014).
context.pull: The original wasn’t forgotten. It was outshouted.
